question: Let $A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & a & a^2 \\ 1 & b & b^2 \\ 1 & c & c^2 \end{bmatrix}$ with $a, b, c$ distinct real numbers. Prove that $|A| = (a-b)(b-c)(c-a)$ and hence discuss the singularity or non-singularity of $A$ for different values of $a, b, c$.
explanation:
Expand $|A|$ along first row:

$|A| = 1 \begin{vmatrix} b & b^2 \\ c & c^2 \end{vmatrix} - a \begin{vmatrix} 1 & b^2 \\ 1 & c^2 \end{vmatrix} + a^2 \begin{vmatrix} 1 & b \\ 1 & c \end{vmatrix}$

$= 1(b c^2 - c b^2) - a(1 \cdot c^2 - 1 \cdot b^2) + a^2(1 \cdot c - 1 \cdot b)$
$= b c^2 - c b^2 - a(c^2 - b^2) + a^2(c - b)$

Rewrite $b c^2 - c b^2 = bc(c-b)$

$- a(c^2 - b^2) = -a(c-b)(c+b)$

$a^2(c-b)$

So:
$|A| = bc(c-b) - a(c-b)(c+b) + a^2(c-b)$
$= (c-b)[bc - a(c+b) + a^2]$

$= (c-b)[bc - a c - a b + a^2]$
$= (c-b)(bc - a b - a c + a^2)$

Now factor $bc - ab - ac + a^2 = (b-a)(c-a)$

So $|A| = (c-b)(b-a)(c-a)$. Changing signs and absolute value as per indexing, $|A| = (a-b)(b-c)(c-a)$.

If any two of $a, b, c$ are equal, determinant vanishes, so $A$ is singular. If $a, b, c$ are all distinct, $A$ is non-singular.

options.B: $|A|=(a-b)(b-c)(c-a)$; hence $A$ is non-singular when $a,b,c$ are distinct and singular when any two of them are equal.
options.D: $|A|=abc$; hence $A$ is singular only when one of $a,b,c$ is zero.
